opus-5.5.text:
I think the reaction would be mixed, and probably a bit skeptical at first. Mathematicians already reason heuristically all the time. If you ask a number theorist why they believe the Riemann hypothesis, they won't say "because nobody has found a counterexample." They'll talk about the primes behaving roughly like a random sequence, about random matrix statistics matching the zeros, about the analogous statement being proved for function fields. Those are real arguments. They just live in people's heads and in informal conversation rather than in anything you can check.

So one reaction would be: "We already do this, why do we need a formalism?" Another would be: "Heuristic arguments are fine as a guide, but the whole point of mathematics is proof, so formalizing the non-proof part sounds like a category error."

I'm sympathetic to both. But I think the case for formalization is roughly the case it has always been. Informal heuristics work well when the people using them have excellent judgment and the problem is close to things they've thought about. They break down when the argument gets long, when you combine many pieces, or when you want to say exactly what assumption you're making when you treat something as random. Formal proof made it possible to build very tall towers of reasoning without them falling over. I'd like something that does the same for "this is probably true because there's no reason for these things to conspire."

And there are real technical puzzles here that mathematicians would find interesting regardless of applications. When is it legitimate to treat a deterministic quantity as random? What happens when someone points out structure you ignored, and how should your estimate update? How do you avoid an argument that seems to prove both a statement and its negation? Those questions have a lot of mathematical content, and I think a good answer would get attention even from people who don't care about the motivation.

My honest guess is that most working mathematicians would be indifferent until it produced something: a heuristic estimate for a problem that people couldn't previously make precise, or a clean account of why certain conjectures are believed. That's the fair bar. For me, the main motivation is less about mathematics and more about AI. If we want to explain why a neural network behaves a certain way, we'll almost never get proofs, so we need some principled notion of a convincing explanation that falls short of proof. Mathematics is the cleanest setting to work out what that would look like.

r001.rationale: It says mathematicians often reason heuristically and gives examples for the Riemann hypothesis, but does not claim that most mathematical claims they believe have compelling heuristic arguments.

r002.rationale: It does not mention unexpected periodic structure in the primes as a possible failure of the heuristic case.

r003.rationale: It does not characterize much mathematical work as ruling out exceptions that could defeat an initial heuristic.

r004.rationale: It predicts that most working mathematicians would be indifferent until formalized heuristics produced a useful result, conveying that they would be largely unimpressed at first.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that most mathematicians would be somewhere between skeptical and uninterested, at least at first, and I don't think that's unreasonable.

Mathematicians already make heuristic arguments all the time. If you ask a number theorist why they believe the Riemann hypothesis, they'll tell you about the numerical evidence, about the function field analogue where it's actually been proven, about random matrix theory and the way the zeros seem to behave like eigenvalues of random Hermitian matrices. Those are heuristic arguments, and people take them seriously. The twin prime conjecture is another good example. Nobody has a proof, but there's a very clean probabilistic heuristic that says primes behave roughly like random numbers with the right density, and that heuristic predicts the number of twin primes up to N, and the prediction matches the data extremely well. So the practice exists. What doesn't exist is any formal account of what makes those arguments good or bad.

So the thing we're trying to do is take that informal practice and ask whether there's a precise standard behind it. When you say "assume the primes behave like random numbers," what exactly are you assuming, and when are you allowed to assume it? When is it legitimate to treat two things as independent that you know are not actually independent? Those questions feel like they should have answers, and right now they don't.

I think the reaction from mathematicians splits into a few camps. One camp says, "this is philosophy, not mathematics, and the interesting thing is proving theorems." And I have some sympathy for that. If you're trying to prove the Riemann hypothesis, a formalized heuristic argument doesn't get you closer to a proof. It just tells you more carefully what you already believed.

A second camp is more interested, because there are real cases where heuristics go wrong, and it would be nice to understand why. The classic example is Skewes' number and the behavior of the prime counting function relative to the logarithmic integral. For a long time the heuristic and the data both suggested one thing, and it turned out to be false eventually, at some astronomically large number. There are also cases where the naive probabilistic heuristic for primes gives the wrong constant and you have to correct it for local obstructions, like divisibility by small primes. A formal theory of heuristic arguments would hopefully explain when you need those corrections and why, rather than leaving it to taste.

And then there's a third reaction, which is the one I'd actually hope for, which is something like, "that's a fine thing to want, but you don't have it yet, come back when you do." Because what we have right now is more like a research program than a result. We can state some desiderata. We can give some toy examples where the formal version agrees with the informal practice. But we don't have a theory that handles the Riemann hypothesis in a way a number theorist would find illuminating. So I'd expect mathematicians to be polite and unimpressed, and I think the burden is on us to produce something that actually explains a case they care about.

The reason I care about this isn't really the Riemann hypothesis, though. It's that if you want to understand what a neural network is doing, you're in a very similar situation. You have an object with a lot of structure, you can't prove things about it, and you want to make arguments like "this part of the network is behaving randomly and this part isn't." The hope is that if you can make that kind of reasoning precise in the mathematical setting, where you have a lot of intuition and a lot of examples to check against, the same machinery carries over to the setting where you don't have that intuition. So mathematicians being skeptical is fine. They're a useful test, not the end goal.

astra-6.text:
I think it would depend a lot on what the formalism actually delivered. Mathematicians already make heuristic arguments, and those arguments can be quite persuasive. The interesting question is whether you can formalize them in a way that adds something to the reasoning people are already doing.

If you had a framework that said, “Here are the assumptions implicit in this heuristic, and here’s why they suggest the Riemann hypothesis,” that seems useful. But you’d then want to understand why you should trust those assumptions. You can move the uncertainty into a formal framework without necessarily resolving it.

I suspect the most compelling demonstration would be to take questions where we don’t yet know the answer, make predictions using the framework, and then have those predictions borne out. Especially if it helped distinguish a good heuristic from a superficially similar argument that gives the wrong answer. At that point, I’d expect mathematicians to be interested, even though they would still distinguish that kind of evidence from a proof.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’d be interested, but a lot would depend on what the formalism actually buys you. Mathematicians already make heuristic arguments about the Riemann hypothesis. The question is whether you can do something more than take the intuitions people already have and put them into a formal language.

If you had a system that made those arguments precise enough that you could identify where two heuristics disagree, or discover that an apparently compelling argument also predicts something false, that seems useful. And if it generated new predictions that subsequently checked out, I think people would take it much more seriously.

There’s still a distinction between saying, “Here’s a very compelling reason to believe the Riemann hypothesis,” and proving it. I don’t expect mathematicians to abandon that distinction. But you could imagine a productive mathematical theory of which heuristic arguments are good, even though its conclusions don’t have the status of theorems about the integers.
